opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, because math is where reinforcement learning has looked the most impressive, and that's exactly why we should be careful about what we conclude from it.

On one hand, the generalization within mathematics is better than many people expected. If you train a model with RL on a certain distribution of competition problems, you often see gains on problems that look quite different on the surface: different topics, different formats, even somewhat harder levels. What the model learns isn't just a set of answers. It learns behaviors: checking its work, trying an alternative approach when one path fails, decomposing a problem, being willing to think longer. Those meta-skills transfer fairly well, and I'd say that's the most important finding of the past year or two.

But there are limits, and I see roughly three.

The first is the reward signal itself. Math works well for RL because answers are verifiable, so you get a clean signal. As soon as you move to problems where the final answer isn't a number, like proofs or open-ended research questions, the reward gets much noisier. The model can learn to produce things that look like valid reasoning without being valid. Generalization is bounded by how good your verifier is.

The second is that RL mostly sharpens what is already in the base model. In many cases it doesn't create fundamentally new knowledge. It raises the probability of reasoning paths the pretrained model could already produce sometimes. So if a problem needs a concept or technique that's basically absent from pretraining, RL alone struggles to get there. The ceiling is still largely set by the base model.

The third is the gap between solving problems and doing mathematics. Competition problems are designed to have clean solutions within a bounded amount of thinking. Real mathematical research involves posing the right questions, building new abstractions, and working over very long horizons with sparse feedback. Current RL setups are not really optimized for that, and I don't think scaling the same recipe will automatically close the gap.

So my overall view is that RL on math generalizes surprisingly well in terms of reasoning habits, but much less in terms of genuinely new capability. The next step is probably better ways to scale the reward: richer verifiers, models that judge their own reasoning more reliably, and longer-horizon tasks. That's where I think a lot of the real progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad transfer and limits to generalization, but does not state that near-perfect performance on one type of math problem need not transfer to near-perfect performance on other types.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the honest answer is that we don't yet know the ceiling, but we have a much better sense of the shape of the problem than we did a year or two ago.

When people talk about RL on math, the first thing to separate is generalization within the distribution you trained on versus generalization across distributions. Within a distribution, RL works almost embarrassingly well. If you take a base model that's reasonably strong, give it verifiable rewards on competition-style problems, and let it do long chain-of-thought, you get large, reliable gains. The model learns to check its work, to backtrack, to try a second approach when the first one stalls. These are real capabilities, not just pattern matching on the answer format.

The harder question is what happens when you move away from that distribution. And here I think there are a few distinct limits.

The first is about the reward signal itself. Math is special because you can verify the final answer cheaply. That's why it was the first domain where RL took off. But the moment you move to problems where verification is expensive or ambiguous, like proofs, or research-level questions where even the problem statement is fuzzy, the signal gets noisier and the model's behavior gets less reliable. So one limit is really a limit of what you can verify, not of RL as a technique.

The second limit is that the base model matters enormously. RL mostly amplifies and sharpens what the pretrained model can already do. It's very good at increasing the probability of behaviors that already exist in the model at low probability. It's much less good at creating genuinely new knowledge. If the base model has never seen a certain class of mathematical objects, RL alone won't teach it. So when we see "generalization," a lot of it is actually the model learning to deploy latent knowledge more effectively, which is valuable but is a different thing from learning new mathematics.

The third limit is more subtle, and it's about what we actually mean by transfer. We've seen that training on math helps on coding, and training on coding helps on math, and sometimes it helps on tasks that look nothing like either. That suggests the model is learning something general, maybe something like how to allocate compute across a long reasoning process, when to be careful, when to explore. But the transfer is uneven. It helps most on tasks that share the same structure of "think for a long time, then produce a checkable answer." It helps much less on tasks that need long-horizon interaction with an environment, or that require the model to gather information it doesn't already have.

So if I try to summarize how I assess the limits: RL has proven that you can scale test-time compute and get real reasoning improvements, and that this reasoning partially transfers. What it hasn't yet proven is that it can take a model beyond the frontier of its own pretraining, or that it works well without a clean reward. Those two things are where I think the next several years of research will go. Better verifiers for open-ended problems, and ways to combine RL with continued learning so the model can actually expand its knowledge rather than just sharpening it.

And I'd add one more thing. We should be careful about reading too much into benchmark saturation. A model scoring very high on competition math doesn't mean we've solved mathematical reasoning. It means we've solved a particular, well-posed slice of it. The interesting failures are still there once you ask the model to do something a mathematician actually does, like decide what question is worth asking.

r001.rationale: The response says high performance on competition math covers only a well-posed slice, and that transfer to other tasks is uneven. This communicates that strong performance on one type of math problem does not guarantee equally strong performance elsewhere.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between getting better at a particular distribution of math problems and learning a reasoning strategy that transfers to new problems. Reinforcement learning can improve the former without necessarily achieving the latter.

In mathematics, we have the advantage that answers are often verifiable, so we can give a relatively clear reward. But a correct answer doesn’t tell us whether the model learned a general method or exploited patterns specific to the training problems. If we train on algebra and see improvements on similar algebra questions, that’s useful, but it’s a limited kind of generalization.

The more interesting test is what happens when you change the structure of the problem, introduce unfamiliar definitions, or require a combination of ideas the model hasn’t practiced together. Can it still make progress? Can it recognize when an approach is failing and try something else?

So I wouldn’t treat higher benchmark scores alone as evidence that reinforcement learning has overcome those limits. I’d want to examine transfer under carefully controlled changes in the problems, while accounting for the model’s prior training and how much computation it gets at inference time. That helps separate improved performance from genuinely broader reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning can improve performance on a particular distribution without learning a strategy that transfers, and describes gains on similar algebra problems as limited generalization. This communicates that strong performance on one problem type need not carry over to others.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between improving performance on a family of problems and generalizing to a fundamentally new kind of problem. Reinforcement learning can make a model much better at finding and checking solutions when the problems have clear rewards. But a higher math benchmark score alone doesn’t tell us how far that improvement transfers.

For example, if you train on certain algebra problems, does the model improve on unfamiliar geometry problems? Can it solve problems that require a concept or a strategy it rarely encountered during training? Those are stronger tests than changing the numbers or wording of a familiar problem.

The limit also depends on the starting model. Pretraining gives it a repertoire of concepts and possible approaches; reinforcement learning changes how effectively it uses and explores that repertoire. It may discover new strategies, but we shouldn’t assume that reliable verification automatically makes those strategies broadly generalizable.

So I would assess generalization by holding out entire problem families, varying difficulty, and measuring performance under comparable inference budgets. The interesting question is whether the model is learning reusable reasoning strategies, and how far those strategies carry beyond the training distribution.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes improvement on a family of problems from generalization to a new kind, and says algebra training may not improve performance on unfamiliar geometry. This communicates that very strong performance on one type need not carry over to other types.
